title: Dolores Huerta dies at 96, leaving a legacy measured in workers’ rights
subtitle: The farmworker organiser helped turn strikes and boycotts into enforceable protections. Her final year also challenged the idea that defending a movement requires women to remain silent about abuse within it.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Dolores Huerta, the labour organiser who helped build the United Farm Workers and brought women’s authority to its bargaining table, died on 28 October at her home in Bakersfield, California. She was 96. Her foundation said she was surrounded by close family.

Her achievements can be measured in the ordinary necessities that make a working life bearable: drinking water, toilets, rest periods, healthcare and protection from pesticides. Reuters’ account of her career records those provisions among the gains secured through the union’s contracts. They made the conditions of agricultural work a matter for negotiation, rather than something workers simply had to endure.

California Governor Gavin Newsom ordered flags flown at half-staff. In a joint statement, he and Jennifer Siebel Newsom recognised Huerta’s work for gender equality, workers’ rights and civil rights, and the generations of organisers who followed her.
The children who changed her work

Born in Dawson, New Mexico, on 10 April 1930, Huerta grew up in Stockton, California. She qualified as a teacher and taught farmworkers’ children. According to the National Park Service’s biography, seeing pupils arrive hungry and without adequate shoes persuaded her that changing their parents’ working conditions could do more than she could accomplish in the classroom alone.
That decision connected a child’s ability to learn with the wages and security of the adults at home. Poverty was not a defect in the child. It was something organised adults could confront.

Huerta and Cesar Chavez established the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. The wider movement had other architects: Filipino workers affiliated with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee began the Delano grape strike in 1965, and Huerta’s organisation joined them. Their organisations subsequently merged.

Keeping those origins visible matters. Labour history becomes misleading when collective action is reduced to a single famous man, or when the woman who negotiated its gains becomes a supporting character.

Huerta’s work helped secure California’s 1975 Agricultural Labor Relations Act, which gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights. Alongside workplace organising, she understood legislation as another way to make employers answerable to the people whose labour sustained their businesses.
Whose safety counts inside a movement?

The National Park Service records that Huerta recognised women farmworkers’ particular exposure to sexual violence and the needs of children working alongside their parents. A campaign for better pay could not, on its own, answer every danger faced by the people earning it.

In March 2026, Huerta publicly said that Chavez had sexually assaulted her in the 1960s. Her foundation’s obituary records her explanation that she had kept the experience secret for decades because she feared damaging the farmworker movement. She spoke after other survivors came forward.
That disclosure belongs in an account of her life because it was her decision to make it public. Remembering her leadership should not require restoring the silence she had broken.

It also presents an institutional challenge that reaches beyond one union. When a cause becomes inseparable from a revered leader, a woman reporting harm can be treated as a threat to everyone’s work. The responsibility runs the other way: organisations must protect the people within them, including when allegations concern those who helped build them.
Huerta’s testimony does not erase the organising of farmworkers or the protections they won. Nor do those achievements provide an answer to her account of abuse. Both belong in the history.
A legacy that requires successors

Her later work through the Dolores Huerta Foundation carried community organising into campaigns concerning schools, water, environmental conditions and civil rights. The foundation says it has trained thousands of residents, many from farmworker families in California’s southern San Joaquin Valley, to take part in decisions affecting their communities.

That is a more demanding inheritance than an inspirational slogan. It asks who can negotiate, who can challenge authority and whether a woman’s voice remains welcome when she says something an institution would rather not hear.

For the families whose lives Huerta sought to improve, remembrance has a practical measure: whether the next generation has the power to secure fair treatment, and the freedom to speak without sacrificing its safety.
The Athena Perspective.
